Because the CCH contains each neuron's auto-correlation convolved with the transmission impulse response, presynaptic bursts inject fast side lobes into the CCH; timescale separation cannot strip them out, so the estimated gain is biased by burstiness rather than by synaptic strength.
quote: Hence, even if an optimal estimate of the other inputs is removed, a CCH between two synaptically-connected neurons will still contain contributions from the ACHs of each neuron.

value: Bursting of the presynaptic neuron produces secondary peaks flanking the causal peak of the CCH, which is the concrete distortion the estimators mistake for transmission.
quote: In addition, the CCH exhibited side lobes: secondary peaks with increased counts on both sides of the causal peak, which are due to the bursting activity of the presynaptic neuron.

value: Deconvolving the two auto-correlation histograms out of the CCH removes the ACH-induced side lobes, leaving a histogram whose causal peak reflects transmission alone before the other-inputs term is subtracted.
quote: In a nutshell, the algorithm mitigates the effect of bursting activity by deconvolving the ACHs from the CCH, resulting in a CCH which does not exhibit ACH-induced side lobes

First, we compared estimation performance with and without deconvolution by computing the mean square error (MSE) for the STG-based methods, for which a ground truth exists (Fig. 4c–e ). We found that deconvolution reduced the MSE for all STG-based methods ( p < 0.001; Wilcoxon’s paired signed-rank test; Fig. 4h ). Of the three STG-based methods, median filtering with deconvolution had the lowest MSE (1.27 × 10 −5 ). Median without deconvolution and jitter with deconvolution had the second and third lowest MSEs, respectively (median: 2.73 × 10 −5 ; jitter with deconvolution: 3.48 × 10 −5 ; jitter: 5.34 × 10 −5 ). Thus, deconvolution reduced the errors approximately two-fold.
